title: DGCA gives SpiceJet seven days to explain cancellations, delays and grounded fleet
dek: The regulator's notice lists ten concerns, from missed schedules and unpaid penalties to uncertainty over insurance cover. The airline, whose market share has fallen below 1%, has approved a plan to raise up to Rs 5,500 crore.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
India's aviation regulator, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), has issued a show-cause notice to SpiceJet over mounting flight cancellations and delays, poor care of stranded passengers and a fleet that is mostly grounded, and has given the airline seven days to reply, according to reports. The notice is dated 17 November and was reported on Friday.

The airline had not publicly commented on the notice by Saturday morning. Its shares fell nearly 5 per cent to Rs 9.74 on the BSE on Friday afternoon, according to reports.

## What the regulator says

The notice sets out a long list of concerns, according to reports:

- a decline in on-time performance and a rise in delays and cancellations, causing hardship to passengers
- not operating the flight schedule the DGCA approved
- inadequate help for passengers during disruptions
- most of its aircraft grounded, with no credible plan to bring them back into service
- uncertainty over the renewal of its mandatory insurance cover
- concerns raised by overseas aviation authorities about disruptions linked to delayed payments to service providers
- failure to pay an earlier penalty despite repeated reminders
- not meeting the eligibility requirements for scheduled international flights
- repeated breaches of the Route Dispersal Guidelines, which oblige airlines to fly a share of their capacity on less profitable routes such as those to the north-east, despite enforcement action and penalties in May

Only about a quarter of SpiceJet's flights ran on time on 19 November, according to reports citing Ministry of Civil Aviation data.

## Background

SpiceJet, once India's second-largest airline, has been in financial difficulty for several years, with aircraft lessors taking it to court over unpaid dues and a large part of its fleet out of service. Its share of the domestic market fell to 0.6 per cent in September from 1.2 per cent in August, according to reports.

The airline's board on 18 November approved a proposal to raise up to Rs 5,500 crore through shares, debt, convertible securities or other instruments, subject to approval by shareholders and regulators, according to reports. It has not said who the investors would be.

A show-cause notice is a formal demand for an explanation before the regulator decides whether to act. Depending on the reply, the DGCA can accept it, impose fines, order the airline to cut its schedule, or in more serious cases restrict its operations. In 2022 the regulator ordered SpiceJet to run only half its approved flights for eight weeks after a series of safety incidents.

## What it means for passengers

For passengers, the immediate concern is whether booked flights will operate. Under the DGCA's passenger charter, travellers whose flights are cancelled are entitled to an alternative flight or a full refund, and in some cases to compensation if they were not told at least two weeks in advance. Passengers can complain through the government's AirSewa portal.

## What happens next

SpiceJet must reply within seven days of the notice, which would be around 24 November. The DGCA will then decide whether to take action.
